medical.title: AI-powered device can fight against malaria by detecting and repelling mosquitoes
medical.summary: A Southampton student who experienced firsthand the devastating impact of malaria while growing up in Cameroon has invented a novel mosquito-repelling gadget.

medical.title: Experiments reveal how DNA-packaging protein mutation promotes breast cancer spread
medical.summary: A research team led by professor Chan Kui-ming from the Department of Biomedical Sciences at CityUHK discovered that H2BE113K, a missense H2B mutation, promotes colony formation and lung metastasis in breast cancer. The research revealed that H2BE113K plays a critical role in chromatin regulation, cellular function and breast cancer progression, shedding light on new targeted therapies for breast cancer.

medical.title: I teach doctors how to interpret test results—and the labels 'normal' and 'abnormal' often hide what matters most
medical.summary: V felt tightness across his chest. His deepest breaths felt shallow. He sought help at an emergency department, where a resident physician found several worrying signs, including swelling of his hands and legs as well as heart enlargement on a chest X-ray.

medical.title: When it comes to health care access, more isn't always better
medical.summary: Hospitals and policymakers routinely face a difficult question when investing in specialized emergency services: Will adding another facility improve care, or would those resources do more good somewhere else?

medical.title: How dyspraxia can exhaust children and exclude them from social activities
medical.summary: Ask a parent of a child with dyspraxia what happens around 4 p.m., and many describe the same scene. Their child has spent a whole school day gripping pencils, fastening buttons and keeping up on the playground. By the time they get home, they are exhausted.

medical.title: New heart transplant proposal could save lives by prioritizing patients' medical urgency
medical.summary: Donor organs are exceedingly scarce, so much so that one in five people on the waiting list for a heart transplant in the U.S. dies or is removed from the list before receiving a transplant.

medical.title: Global dementia study reveals 11.4 million new cases in 2023—projected to more than double by 2050
medical.summary: International research has produced some of the most comprehensive and comparable estimates of new dementia cases worldwide, revealing that an estimated 11.4 million people developed dementia in 2023—a figure projected to rise to 24.7 million a year by 2050. The study, published in JAMA Neurology, analyzed data from 38,418 people across 22 population-based studies spanning 18 countries and territories on six continents.

medical.title: Having someone to talk to linked to better mental health among LGBQ+ teens
medical.summary: Gay or bisexual teens who have someone to turn to with a serious problem have significantly better mental health outcomes than those who don't, according to a new study from Tulane University researchers.

medical.title: Healthy diet during pregnancy associated with reduced risk of infant colic and eczema
medical.summary: Infants born to mothers who ate a healthy, Mediterranean-style diet during pregnancy were at lower risk for colic and eczema, according to a new study by researchers at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute. The researchers also found that regularly consuming seafood during pregnancy helped lower an infant's risk for these conditions.

medical.title: Psilocybin providers follow safety guidelines, study finds
medical.summary: A new study has found that Oregon's licensed psilocybin centers largely follow recommended safety guidelines, offering reassurance about how the first regulated psilocybin programs in the U.S. function in practice—though the cost of treatment may keep it out of reach for many.

medical.title: Living with ringing in your ears? Updated guideline supports a personalized, evidence-based approach to tinnitus
medical.summary: The American Academy of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF) today published the Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG): Tinnitus Update in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, and for some it brings significant anxiety, depression, sleep problems and difficulty functioning. Yet the care patients receive varies widely, both in the treatments offered and in how closely clinicians follow published guidelines.

medical.title: Connecting veterans' PTSD, unmet social needs to cognitive impairment and dementia
medical.summary: A multi-institutional research team recently reported that veterans with both PTSD and unmet social needs appear to have higher rates of dementia or cognitive impairment years later. The study involved 3,817,970 veterans—and, therefore, millions of data points—so the team relied on support from researchers in the Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences (CICS) at UMass Amherst, who helped process the large amounts of data needed for the study.

medical.title: Relationship study finds helping dementia patient supports even their spousal caregiver
medical.summary: Just as a fleet of ships moves across the ocean—the flagship in the lead as other vessels circle around it—people move through life with a social convoy around them, closest confidants shifting as a person's season of life changes.

medical.title: Think cannabis helps you sleep better? Think again
medical.summary: Millions of Americans use cannabis products as sleep aids, but a new Northwestern Medicine study suggests marijuana may not improve sleep the way many people believe it does.

medical.title: For your health—making the switch to healthier fats
medical.summary: Choosing healthy fats is an important part of healthy eating. And that's good news for a lot of reasons. Fats can add flavor and great texture to foods, boosting our enjoyment. They can help us feel fuller longer, so we don't get too hungry between meals. And, if we choose certain types of fats, they can do all that—plus be really good for us.

medical.title: Treating insomnia could be key to reducing symptoms of depression
medical.summary: Researchers have found that treating insomnia can also help reduce symptoms of depression, with participants in a new study reporting improvements in both conditions. Led by Vanika Lall, clinical associate professor Melissa Ree and emeritus professor Romola Bucks, from The University of Western Australia's School of Psychological Science, the study published in Behaviour Research and Therapy found insomnia therapy may hold the key to lasting recovery from depression.

medical.title: Sitting for longer than 25 minutes may be a tipping point for worse health outcomes
medical.summary: It's widely accepted that sitting around for a long time is bad for us—but Swinburne research has revealed that the time to get moving may come sooner than you think.

medical.title: Loneliness drives biggest quality-of-life drop for young Australians
medical.summary: While older adults often get the most attention for being isolated, young people are losing more of their quality of life—such as feeling healthy, happy and able to enjoy daily activities—because they feel lonely.

medical.title: Rise in cannabis-related psychosis hospitalizations sparks concern in Victoria
medical.summary: New research from Monash University shows cannabis-related hospital admissions have risen sharply across Victoria over the past decade, highlighting growing concerns about cannabis-related psychosis and the burden on the state's hospitals.

medical.title: Two-trigger drugs target 'zombie' cancer cells with sharper aim
medical.summary: Stopping a cancer cell from dividing does not necessarily make it harmless. Chemotherapy can leave behind living, senescent cells. These 'zombie' cells can release inflammatory signals, helping tumors resist treatment. Drugs that eliminate these lingering cells could help, but they can also harm other cells.

medical.title: Researchers identify specific brain circuits associated with anxiety in adolescents
medical.summary: Adolescence is a sensitive period for brain development and mental health, though the connection between the two is not fully understood. New research published in Imaging Neuroscience identifies a link between anxiety and specific brain circuits, which could become the targets of precision interventions to improve mental health outcomes in youth.

medical.title: Putting a ring on it: the plan to green London’s beloved edges
medical.summary: Ten million people will benefit from a more biodiverse capital, say the organisers of an ambitious project to reconnect its wilder spaces The post Putting a ring on it: the plan to green London’s beloved edges appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
medical.summary: Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms.

medical.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

medical.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.

science.title: Mangroves shield coasts from waves, but seedlings need calm waters to take root
science.summary: Mangrove forests, which are widespread along subtropical and tropical coasts, play a vital role in coastal protection, as they dampen the force of waves and storm surges. They also naturally store carbon in the soil and are home to a wide variety of living organisms.

science.title: Conservation parks don't have to be vast—as one tiny grasshopper reminds us
science.summary: A vast stretch of land where animals roam widely and plants grow freely. That's what most people would picture if they thought of a conservation area.

science.title: How nature lovers can aid ecology with an assist from AI
science.summary: Millions of people worldwide, likely without realizing it, are capturing rare and valuable data that can help researchers assess trends in ecosystem health. Such data, however, are hidden in an ocean of comments on free online platforms like eBird and iNaturalist used by birdwatchers and other nature enthusiasts.

science.title: African genomics research is growing: What countries are doing to connect genetic data and health care
science.summary: Much of what scientists know about how genetic differences affect health comes from studying populations outside Africa. This matters because genetic information is increasingly being used to understand disease, interpret genetic tests and, in some cases, guide treatment.

science.title: One step closer to quantum computers that can correct their own mistakes
science.summary: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.

science.title: Universities are making different choices about AI. How will they fit with their public missions?
science.summary: Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from an emerging technology to one that is forcing universities to make consequential choices.

science.title: ALMA catches a dying star mid-transformation, with a ring from its last outburst
science.summary: Astronomers have used radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to catch a dying star in the middle of a dramatic transformation, and the data show a ring that records its final outburst. The new research was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18. The paper has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal.

science.title: Identity develops well into adulthood and is linked to better mental well-being
science.summary: Identity development is not limited to adolescence, a recent study from the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, shows. Researchers found that identity developed positively from age 27 to 61. A more positively developed identity was associated with higher levels of mental well-being.

science.title: 'Molecular sunscreen' may explain why DNA uses thymine despite its vulnerability to UV damage
science.summary: Scientists have long sought to understand the complex origins of intelligent life. It remains unclear how biological systems not only formed but survived and persisted under the extreme conditions of primordial Earth's hostile climate. Now, researchers at Texas A&M University are using light-based technologies to uncover new clues to help solve this evolutionary puzzle.

science.title: The Preliminary Lunar Science Report for Artemis II is out
science.summary: On April 1, 2026, the crew of the Artemis II mission launched into space atop NASA's Space Launch System (SLS). Roughly 3 1/2 hours after launch, the rocket's upper stage separated from the Orion spacecraft (Integrity), and astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen began their nearly 10-day journey around the moon.

science.title: Some house cats carry a gut parasite that can infect humans, study finds
science.summary: Giardia duodenalis is a microscopic, flagellated parasite that often calls the human and animal gut its home. In most cases, it coexists harmlessly with its host, and most infected pets and people show no signs of illness. However, when it becomes pathogenic, it can cause diarrhea, digestive issues or weight loss.

science.title: Atypical B cells shift immune roles as they develop, malaria study finds
science.summary: B cells are an important part of the immune system and help the body recognize and fight infections. A group of B cells known as atypical B cells has attracted considerable interest among researchers in recent years. They occur in several infections, but also in connection with vaccinations and certain inflammatory diseases. Despite extensive research, it has long remained unclear how these cells arise and what function they serve.

science.title: As the school year settles in, making room for the arts can support everyday well‑being
science.summary: As the days darken, making more room for arts-based practices and experiences is one way to bring useful, interesting or sustaining activities into the seasons ahead.

science.title: Ball or strike? Why the count may change what a baseball umpire sees
science.summary: In baseball, a borderline pitch is more likely to be called a strike when the batter has three balls and no strikes than when the count is no balls and two strikes. The official strike zone hasn't changed. The umpire's judgment has.

science.title: AI platform and database map protein phase separation across species
science.summary: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have developed an AI-powered database and a platform that could enable researchers to more accurately predict which proteins undergo phase separation—a process through which proteins in cells separate like oil droplets in water.

science.title: Why a tiny number of venture capitalists capture almost all the profit
science.summary: Beyond a handful of big names, most venture capitalists are relatively unknown. Who are they, and what distinguishes the superstars from the rest?

science.title: New sensor uses slowed light to detect gravitational pull of tiny objects
science.summary: Gravity, the attraction between objects with mass, is the weakest of the four fundamental forces governing physical processes. Detecting the tiny gravitational pull of objects that are just a few millimeters in size and have a very small mass is extremely challenging.

science.title: AI system could transform rabies testing around the world
science.summary: Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to the world's first AI system for this purpose, developed by researchers at the University of Surrey's Institute for People-Centered AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA).

science.title: Study explores why Indigenous communities may accept oil extraction despite its harms
science.summary: The uneven distribution of oil extraction's impacts and benefits helps explain why some Indigenous communities accept it, newly published research shows.

science.title: Model links course design, psychological safety and guided AI use
science.summary: University of Phoenix researchers have published a new peer-reviewed study examining how stress, self-regulation, resilience, belonging, psychological safety and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) interact in the experiences of nontraditional online students. The article, "Designing for Persistence in Online Higher Education: A Trauma-Informed, GenAI-Integrated Model for Non-Traditional Learners," was published in Innovative Higher Education.

science.title: AI platforms offer promise in limiting the illegal wildlife trade
science.summary: New University of Kent research has found promising signs that AI platforms have the potential to limit the illegal wildlife trade. The research paper titled "Assessing safeguards against the illegal wildlife trade on AI platforms" is published in Conservation Biology.

science.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
science.summary: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

science.title: Hurricane Simon churns off Mexican coast after shift in course
science.summary: Hurricane Simon shifted track slightly on Sunday and was forecast to skirt Mexico's west coast without making landfall, while packing heavy rain and severe winds.

science.title: World leaders urged to 'course correct' as UN nature goals fall short
science.summary: Nations are steeling for a disappointing report card at this month's U.N. biodiversity summit, with governments falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.

science.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
science.summary: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.

environment.title: Brazilian ranchers block government officials from demarcating Indigenous land
environment.summary: Since Sept. 23, a group of rural producers has maintained a blockade on the road to the Paquiçamba Indigenous Land in the Volta Grande do Xingu region of Brazil’s Pará state. The blockade is supported by local politicians and aims to prevent government officials from physically demarcating the land traditionally occupied by the Juruna (Yudjá) […]

environment.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
environment.summary: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

environment.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

environment.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
environment.summary: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.

environment.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
environment.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

environment.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
environment.summary: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils.

environment.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
environment.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

environment.title: Stonehenge’s 6-ton altar stone may have traveled from Scotland by glacier
environment.summary: Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone may have been carried from Scotland to Dogger Bank by glaciers before prehistoric people transported it hundreds of kilometers to Salisbury Plain. The possible multistage journey suggests remarkable organization and raises the possibility that the stone was valued long before it became part of Stonehenge.

environment.title: Scientists say a critical Atlantic Ocean current is weakening and the effects could be global
environment.summary: Scientists have found strong observational evidence that a key part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation has been weakening across a wide stretch of ocean for nearly two decades. The slowdown could eventually reshape weather patterns, rainfall, storms, winters, and coastal sea levels around the Atlantic.

mix_items.summary: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.

mix_items.summary: Astronomers have used radio observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to catch a dying star in the middle of a dramatic transformation, and the data show a ring that records its final outburst. The new research was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 18. The paper has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal.

mix_items.title: When it comes to health care access, more isn't always better
mix_items.summary: Hospitals and policymakers routinely face a difficult question when investing in specialized emergency services: Will adding another facility improve care, or would those resources do more good somewhere else?

mix_items.title: How dyspraxia can exhaust children and exclude them from social activities
mix_items.summary: Ask a parent of a child with dyspraxia what happens around 4 p.m., and many describe the same scene. Their child has spent a whole school day gripping pencils, fastening buttons and keeping up on the playground. By the time they get home, they are exhausted.

mix_items.title: New heart transplant proposal could save lives by prioritizing patients' medical urgency
mix_items.summary: Donor organs are exceedingly scarce, so much so that one in five people on the waiting list for a heart transplant in the U.S. dies or is removed from the list before receiving a transplant.

mix_items.title: Identity develops well into adulthood and is linked to better mental well-being
mix_items.summary: Identity development is not limited to adolescence, a recent study from the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, shows. Researchers found that identity developed positively from age 27 to 61. A more positively developed identity was associated with higher levels of mental well-being.

mix_items.title: Global dementia study reveals 11.4 million new cases in 2023—projected to more than double by 2050
mix_items.summary: International research has produced some of the most comprehensive and comparable estimates of new dementia cases worldwide, revealing that an estimated 11.4 million people developed dementia in 2023—a figure projected to rise to 24.7 million a year by 2050. The study, published in JAMA Neurology, analyzed data from 38,418 people across 22 population-based studies spanning 18 countries and territories on six continents.

mix_items.title: Having someone to talk to linked to better mental health among LGBQ+ teens
mix_items.summary: Gay or bisexual teens who have someone to turn to with a serious problem have significantly better mental health outcomes than those who don't, according to a new study from Tulane University researchers.

mix_items.title: Healthy diet during pregnancy associated with reduced risk of infant colic and eczema
mix_items.summary: Infants born to mothers who ate a healthy, Mediterranean-style diet during pregnancy were at lower risk for colic and eczema, according to a new study by researchers at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute. The researchers also found that regularly consuming seafood during pregnancy helped lower an infant's risk for these conditions.

mix_items.title: Psilocybin providers follow safety guidelines, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study has found that Oregon's licensed psilocybin centers largely follow recommended safety guidelines, offering reassurance about how the first regulated psilocybin programs in the U.S. function in practice—though the cost of treatment may keep it out of reach for many.

mix_items.title: Living with ringing in your ears? Updated guideline supports a personalized, evidence-based approach to tinnitus
mix_items.summary: The American Academy of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF) today published the Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG): Tinnitus Update in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, and for some it brings significant anxiety, depression, sleep problems and difficulty functioning. Yet the care patients receive varies widely, both in the treatments offered and in how closely clinicians follow published guidelines.

mix_items.title: 'Molecular sunscreen' may explain why DNA uses thymine despite its vulnerability to UV damage
mix_items.summary: Scientists have long sought to understand the complex origins of intelligent life. It remains unclear how biological systems not only formed but survived and persisted under the extreme conditions of primordial Earth's hostile climate. Now, researchers at Texas A&M University are using light-based technologies to uncover new clues to help solve this evolutionary puzzle.

mix_items.title: The Preliminary Lunar Science Report for Artemis II is out
mix_items.summary: On April 1, 2026, the crew of the Artemis II mission launched into space atop NASA's Space Launch System (SLS). Roughly 3 1/2 hours after launch, the rocket's upper stage separated from the Orion spacecraft (Integrity), and astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen began their nearly 10-day journey around the moon.

mix_items.title: Connecting veterans' PTSD, unmet social needs to cognitive impairment and dementia
mix_items.summary: A multi-institutional research team recently reported that veterans with both PTSD and unmet social needs appear to have higher rates of dementia or cognitive impairment years later. The study involved 3,817,970 veterans—and, therefore, millions of data points—so the team relied on support from researchers in the Manning College of Information and Computer Sciences (CICS) at UMass Amherst, who helped process the large amounts of data needed for the study.

mix_items.title: Some house cats carry a gut parasite that can infect humans, study finds
mix_items.summary: Giardia duodenalis is a microscopic, flagellated parasite that often calls the human and animal gut its home. In most cases, it coexists harmlessly with its host, and most infected pets and people show no signs of illness. However, when it becomes pathogenic, it can cause diarrhea, digestive issues or weight loss.

mix_items.title: Relationship study finds helping dementia patient supports even their spousal caregiver
mix_items.summary: Just as a fleet of ships moves across the ocean—the flagship in the lead as other vessels circle around it—people move through life with a social convoy around them, closest confidants shifting as a person's season of life changes.

mix_items.title: Think cannabis helps you sleep better? Think again
mix_items.summary: Millions of Americans use cannabis products as sleep aids, but a new Northwestern Medicine study suggests marijuana may not improve sleep the way many people believe it does.

mix_items.title: Atypical B cells shift immune roles as they develop, malaria study finds
mix_items.summary: B cells are an important part of the immune system and help the body recognize and fight infections. A group of B cells known as atypical B cells has attracted considerable interest among researchers in recent years. They occur in several infections, but also in connection with vaccinations and certain inflammatory diseases. Despite extensive research, it has long remained unclear how these cells arise and what function they serve.

mix_items.title: As the school year settles in, making room for the arts can support everyday well‑being
mix_items.summary: As the days darken, making more room for arts-based practices and experiences is one way to bring useful, interesting or sustaining activities into the seasons ahead.

mix_items.title: Ball or strike? Why the count may change what a baseball umpire sees
mix_items.summary: In baseball, a borderline pitch is more likely to be called a strike when the batter has three balls and no strikes than when the count is no balls and two strikes. The official strike zone hasn't changed. The umpire's judgment has.

mix_items.title: For your health—making the switch to healthier fats
mix_items.summary: Choosing healthy fats is an important part of healthy eating. And that's good news for a lot of reasons. Fats can add flavor and great texture to foods, boosting our enjoyment. They can help us feel fuller longer, so we don't get too hungry between meals. And, if we choose certain types of fats, they can do all that—plus be really good for us.

mix_items.title: AI platform and database map protein phase separation across species
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have developed an AI-powered database and a platform that could enable researchers to more accurately predict which proteins undergo phase separation—a process through which proteins in cells separate like oil droplets in water.

mix_items.title: Why a tiny number of venture capitalists capture almost all the profit
mix_items.summary: Beyond a handful of big names, most venture capitalists are relatively unknown. Who are they, and what distinguishes the superstars from the rest?

mix_items.title: Treating insomnia could be key to reducing symptoms of depression
mix_items.summary: Researchers have found that treating insomnia can also help reduce symptoms of depression, with participants in a new study reporting improvements in both conditions. Led by Vanika Lall, clinical associate professor Melissa Ree and emeritus professor Romola Bucks, from The University of Western Australia's School of Psychological Science, the study published in Behaviour Research and Therapy found insomnia therapy may hold the key to lasting recovery from depression.

mix_items.title: Sitting for longer than 25 minutes may be a tipping point for worse health outcomes
mix_items.summary: It's widely accepted that sitting around for a long time is bad for us—but Swinburne research has revealed that the time to get moving may come sooner than you think.

mix_items.title: Loneliness drives biggest quality-of-life drop for young Australians
mix_items.summary: While older adults often get the most attention for being isolated, young people are losing more of their quality of life—such as feeling healthy, happy and able to enjoy daily activities—because they feel lonely.

mix_items.title: New sensor uses slowed light to detect gravitational pull of tiny objects
mix_items.summary: Gravity, the attraction between objects with mass, is the weakest of the four fundamental forces governing physical processes. Detecting the tiny gravitational pull of objects that are just a few millimeters in size and have a very small mass is extremely challenging.

mix_items.title: AI system could transform rabies testing around the world
mix_items.summary: Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to the world's first AI system for this purpose, developed by researchers at the University of Surrey's Institute for People-Centered AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA).

mix_items.title: Rise in cannabis-related psychosis hospitalizations sparks concern in Victoria
mix_items.summary: New research from Monash University shows cannabis-related hospital admissions have risen sharply across Victoria over the past decade, highlighting growing concerns about cannabis-related psychosis and the burden on the state's hospitals.

mix_items.title: Two-trigger drugs target 'zombie' cancer cells with sharper aim
mix_items.summary: Stopping a cancer cell from dividing does not necessarily make it harmless. Chemotherapy can leave behind living, senescent cells. These 'zombie' cells can release inflammatory signals, helping tumors resist treatment. Drugs that eliminate these lingering cells could help, but they can also harm other cells.

mix_items.title: Study explores why Indigenous communities may accept oil extraction despite its harms
mix_items.summary: The uneven distribution of oil extraction's impacts and benefits helps explain why some Indigenous communities accept it, newly published research shows.

mix_items.title: Model links course design, psychological safety and guided AI use
mix_items.summary: University of Phoenix researchers have published a new peer-reviewed study examining how stress, self-regulation, resilience, belonging, psychological safety and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) interact in the experiences of nontraditional online students. The article, "Designing for Persistence in Online Higher Education: A Trauma-Informed, GenAI-Integrated Model for Non-Traditional Learners," was published in Innovative Higher Education.

mix_items.title: AI platforms offer promise in limiting the illegal wildlife trade
mix_items.summary: New University of Kent research has found promising signs that AI platforms have the potential to limit the illegal wildlife trade. The research paper titled "Assessing safeguards against the illegal wildlife trade on AI platforms" is published in Conservation Biology.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify specific brain circuits associated with anxiety in adolescents
mix_items.summary: Adolescence is a sensitive period for brain development and mental health, though the connection between the two is not fully understood. New research published in Imaging Neuroscience identifies a link between anxiety and specific brain circuits, which could become the targets of precision interventions to improve mental health outcomes in youth.

mix_items.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
mix_items.summary: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

mix_items.title: Putting a ring on it: the plan to green London’s beloved edges
mix_items.summary: Ten million people will benefit from a more biodiverse capital, say the organisers of an ambitious project to reconnect its wilder spaces The post Putting a ring on it: the plan to green London’s beloved edges appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
mix_items.summary: Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

mix_items.title: Hurricane Simon churns off Mexican coast after shift in course
mix_items.summary: Hurricane Simon shifted track slightly on Sunday and was forecast to skirt Mexico's west coast without making landfall, while packing heavy rain and severe winds.

mix_items.title: World leaders urged to 'course correct' as UN nature goals fall short
mix_items.summary: Nations are steeling for a disappointing report card at this month's U.N. biodiversity summit, with governments falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
mix_items.summary: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.

mix_items.title: Brazilian ranchers block government officials from demarcating Indigenous land
mix_items.summary: Since Sept. 23, a group of rural producers has maintained a blockade on the road to the Paquiçamba Indigenous Land in the Volta Grande do Xingu region of Brazil’s Pará state. The blockade is supported by local politicians and aims to prevent government officials from physically demarcating the land traditionally occupied by the Juruna (Yudjá) […]

mix_items.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
mix_items.summary: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.

mix_items.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet.

mix_items.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
mix_items.summary: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.

mix_items.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

mix_items.title: A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
mix_items.summary: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils.

mix_items.title: These tropical trees breathe at night to survive drought
mix_items.summary: Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

mix_items.title: Stonehenge’s 6-ton altar stone may have traveled from Scotland by glacier
mix_items.summary: Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone may have been carried from Scotland to Dogger Bank by glaciers before prehistoric people transported it hundreds of kilometers to Salisbury Plain. The possible multistage journey suggests remarkable organization and raises the possibility that the stone was valued long before it became part of Stonehenge.

mix_items.title: Scientists say a critical Atlantic Ocean current is weakening and the effects could be global
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found strong observational evidence that a key part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation has been weakening across a wide stretch of ocean for nearly two decades. The slowdown could eventually reshape weather patterns, rainfall, storms, winters, and coastal sea levels around the Atlantic.
